articles.title: ‘I never imagined I’d end up in this situation’:  IIT Kanpur alumnus, 61, struggles to find a US tech job for nearly two years, turns to gig work and considers…
articles.summary: For more than two decades, Gautam Dev built his career in the US technology industry, expecting his experience to help him navigate the ups and downs of
articles.body: For more than two decades, Gautam Dev built his career in the US technology industry, expecting his experience to help him navigate the ups and downs of the job market. But at 61, the IIT Kanpur alumnus finds himself struggling to secure a full-time position, pay rent and manage mounting bills. Now, he is considering returning to India, where he lived before moving to the US more than two decades ago.Dev shared his experience in an as-told-to essay published by Business Insider. His difficulties began in September 2024, when his employer told him he would have to relocate to another state to keep his software engineering job. Rather than move, he decided to leave the job and look for another opportunity while staying in Dallas, Texas.What he expected to be a temporary gap between jobs has turned into a prolonged struggle. Despite years of experience, applications and interviews, he has yet to secure another full-time role. “In 2024, while working as a software engineer for an IT company in Dallas, I was told I'd have to relocate to another state to keep my job. That September, I decided to quit my job, stay in Dallas, and look for a new role. That decision became a disaster,” Dev told Business Insider. His account has also been reported by Indian media outlets.When experience did not translate into a new jobDev said he had faced employment gaps earlier in his career, but they had usually lasted only a few months before he found another position. This time, the search has been markedly different. He initially looked for vacancies, primarily through LinkedIn, and contacted people in his professional network. However, many told him their companies were not hiring. Some said their jobs had become more demanding but that they were reluctant to leave because they feared they might struggle to find another position.Dev did manage to secure interviews, including multiple rounds with the same company. Yet none led to a job offer. “I didn’t realise how difficult finding another job would be,” he said. He believes several factors may be affecting his prospects, including his age, the length of his employment gap and changes in the technology industry. Dev said he had come across openings in artificial intelligence engineering but did not feel confident applying for roles that required experience he lacked. His account does not establish why individual employers rejected his applications. However, it reflects the uncertainty he has experienced while trying to return to full-time employment after decades in the industry.From software engineering to gig workAfter months of applications and unsuccessful interviews, Dev decided to spend less time actively searching for full-time work and more time trying to earn money. “I need to spend that time earning money instead,” he said. He tried day trading, which initially went well before his fortunes changed. He also turned to gig work through platforms such as Uber, DoorDash and Walmart Spark. The work has provided some income, but not enough to cover his expenses comfortably.Dev said his physical limitations also restrict the kind of delivery work he can take on, as he cannot carry heavy items. With his earnings falling short, his financial position has become increasingly difficult. He has drawn down his savings and accumulated credit card debt while trying to keep up with rent and other bills. “Even with gig work, it's become difficult to keep paying the bills. I've had to drain my savings and take on a lot of credit card debt,” he said.Finding cheaper accommodation has also proved difficult to navigate. Dev would like to move to a less expensive place in Dallas but worries that a landlord could ask for proof of employment and a steady income. Moving would also take time away from delivery work, affecting the money he can earn.A fundraiser, Social Security and the possibility of returning to IndiaIn January, Dev started a GoFundMe fundraiser to help pay his bills. According to his account, it raised more than $9,000, which went towards his expenses. “It was hard to ask people for money, and not everyone has been supportive. But some people have been really nice and generous,” he said. He is now looking towards another potential source of income. Dev expects to become eligible for Social Security benefits when he turns 62 in January 2027. He hopes the payments, combined with whatever he can earn through gig work, will ease some of the financial pressure.Returning to India is also under consideration. Dev lived in India before moving to the US more than two decades ago and eventually becoming an American citizen. However, he has said he is not rushing into a decision, as relocating would require time and careful planning. For now, he intends to continue gig work while weighing his options. The prospect of leaving the US after building a career there marks a difficult turning point for someone who had expected his professional experience to provide greater security. “I never imagined I’d end up in this situation, but here I am,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Maine was replacing an aging river bridge when part of the new structure collapsed during a concrete pour and injured workers; two months later, crews are dismantling the damaged spans before construction resumes
articles.summary: Demolition crews in Maine have started removing damaged parts of a new river bridge that partly collapsed while workers were pouring concrete.
articles.body: Demolition crews in Maine have started removing damaged parts of a new river bridge that partly collapsed while workers were pouring concrete. The incident sent injured workers to hospital and brought a major bridge replacement project to a halt. Engineers and heavy equipment operators are cutting apart and removing damaged sections of the new Llewellyn Estes Bridge over the Stillwater River in Old Town. According to updates published by the Maine Department of Transportation (MaineDOT), contractors are using special heavy machinery to separate damaged sections from the supporting piers and abutments. They are then lifting the broken pieces out of the river. The demolition follows an incident on August 13, when a newly built section of the bridge suddenly failed as workers poured wet concrete for the new bridge deck.Controlled dismantling and river cleanupDemolition work began on Tuesday, 13 October. Crews must break the collapsed structure into smaller pieces while working above the water. Officials at MaineDOT confirmed that heavy equipment operators are carefully lifting the broken materials out of the Stillwater River. The debris will then be taken to dry land for processing and disposal. Engineers planned the slow, careful removal process to protect workers and avoid damaging nearby concrete piers and abutments that survived the original collapse. To make room for the large cranes and equipment needed for the work, state transport officials introduced daytime traffic closures on the nearby temporary bridge carrying Stillwater Avenue. Under guidelines issued by MaineDOT, the temporary bridge will close at intervals between 9 am and 3 pm. Transport officials have set up a signed detour directing drivers along Bennoch Road, North Main Street, and College Avenue while heavy lifting takes place above the road. Safety teams said the need for road closures would decrease as demolition work moved downstream and farther away from the active detour lane.Collapse during concrete deck pourThe incident happened on 13 August 2026 during construction of a modern replacement for the ageing Llewellyn Estes Bridge. The bridge carries Stillwater Avenue over two channels of the Stillwater River. As workers poured wet concrete onto the bridge deck, one of the main spans suddenly failed and collapsed into the river below. Several construction workers were injured in the fall and needed immediate medical checks and treatment. The new bridge was still under construction and closed to public traffic when the collapse happened. Drivers were already using a nearby temporary bridge built by MaineDOT to keep traffic moving through Old Town. After the accident, state inspectors examined the temporary bridge to check whether the collapse of the nearby structure had affected its safety. The inspection confirmed that the temporary bridge remained stable and safe for public use.Multi-agency forensic investigationState transport officials launched a detailed investigation to find out what caused the bridge deck to fail. MaineDOT partnered with the Federal Highway Administration's Turner-Fairbank Highway Research Center to carry out the investigation and provide independent structural analysis and technical support. The review team also includes the main contractor, Reed & Reed, Inc., the beam designer and manufacturer, Basalt Engineering International, and the Advanced Structures and Composites Center. Investigation teams inspected the site and collected material samples from the debris. They are reviewing design calculations, records of how materials were made, and the procedures used to pour the concrete. In an official statement released after the incident, MaineDOT officials stressed that a full investigation was needed before construction could safely restart. "MaineDOT and its partners continue to collect and review all available information and data related to the design, fabrication, and construction of the new Llewellyn Estes Bridge," the department said in an official public statement. "This information gathering is part of a thorough and comprehensive review to determine the factors that led to the failure of one of the new spans during concrete placement of the new bridge deck."Next steps for bridge replacementThe Llewellyn Estes Bridge replacement is part of Maine's wider infrastructure improvement programme. The programme aims to replace ageing river crossings across Penobscot County. Once demolition crews finish removing the damaged concrete and support beams from the Stillwater River, engineers will examine the exposed foundation piers to assess their condition. Plans to rebuild the bridge will depend on the findings of the joint investigation led by MaineDOT and federal highway investigators. State transport officials said public safety remains the main priority. They will provide further traffic updates and details about the project schedule as the cleanup work progresses.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Suvendu Adhikari in Delhi for BIMSTEC dinner meet

articles.title: 'His blood splattered over everybody': US man dies after falling from roller coaster ride
articles.summary: A 42-year-old man died after being thrown from a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia near Atlanta, with witnesses saying he struck other riders
articles.body: A 42-year-old man died after being thrown from a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia near Atlanta, with witnesses saying he struck other riders before falling to the ground, the Associated Press reported.The deceased was identified as Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, an Atlanta resident, by Cobb County police. According to news agency AP, authorities said multiple people were injured but did not provide details about their injuries or conditions. The department's Major Crimes Unit is investigating the incident.Witnesses told local media that the incident occurred on Goliath, a roller coaster that reaches speeds of around 70 mph and rises to a height of about 200 feet. The ride was temporarily halted following the incident, with passengers seen being evacuated and walking down a steep incline.‘His blood splattered over everybody’: Witnesses recount horrorA woman who was at the park told Atlanta-based news outlet 11Alive that she saw the man fall from the ride and hit another passenger."A man fell off the Goliath ride," she said, adding that he struck a girl sitting two rows ahead of her near the point where photographs are taken during the ride.She said the man hit the roller coaster car several times before falling. "His blood splattered over everybody, and his body fell behind one of the haunted attractions," she told 11Alive.The woman said passengers were made to wait for some time before they were allowed to exit the ride.Another witness, Logan Conner, who was riding Goliath with his fiancée, described seeing the man come out of his seat."The man started levitating in the air sideways," he told NBC. "We made direct eye contact with him."Another couple who witnessed the incident said the roller coaster struck the man several times before he was thrown from the ride."It went from having a great time to just screaming, 'Oh my God, what is happening,'" the woman said, describing the sudden shift from excitement to panic.Nine similar roller coasters shut as precautionSix Flags Entertainment Corp. temporarily shut nine similar roller coasters across six amusement parks in North America following the incident, citing an abundance of caution.The rides include Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America, Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain, Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure, Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada's Wonderland, Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds, and Orion and Diamondback at Kings Island.A company spokesperson said park staff and local authorities responded immediately and that the company was cooperating with the investigation."We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," the spokesperson said, adding that support was being provided to affected visitors and employees.The park was already scheduled to be closed on Tuesday. Six Flags has not announced when the temporarily suspended rides will reopen.Goliath, which opened in 2006, features a drop of more than 200 feet and reaches speeds of around 70 mph, according to the park's website.Death follows safety concerns over another Six Flags rideThe fatal incident comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in California announced the permanent retirement of its X2 roller coaster following lawsuits alleging that riders had suffered serious brain injuries.The ride, which features rotating seats, a 215-foot drop and multiple flips, had been closed since July 12. One lawsuit involved a rider who allegedly suffered a catastrophic brain injury, while the park also settled a wrongful-death lawsuit involving a 22-year-old man who died after riding X2 in 2022.The latest incident has prompted fresh scrutiny of roller coaster safety as authorities investigate what caused Kariem to fall from the Goliath ride.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2014, Tony Robbins turned a childhood memory of his struggling family receiving groceries from a stranger into Feeding America’s 100 Million Meals Challenge; expanded later, it reached 1 billion meals in 2023
articles.summary: Tony Robbins’ hunger-relief work began not with a fundraising campaign, but with a memory from his childhood.
articles.body: Tony Robbins’ hunger-relief work began not with a fundraising campaign, but with a memory from his childhood. As the motivational speaker and author has recounted, his family was struggling financially when he was about 11 years old, and a stranger arrived at their home with groceries and a frozen turkey for Thanksgiving. The experience stayed with him and later became part of the inspiration for his partnership with Feeding America, the US-based hunger-relief organisation.In 2014, Robbins and Feeding America launched the 100 Million Meals Challenge, an initiative aimed at helping families facing food insecurity. What began as a campaign to provide millions of meals subsequently expanded into a much larger commitment. In 2017, the partners announced a billion-meal goal, and in November 2023, Feeding America said the challenge had surpassed its target nearly two years ahead of schedule. The organisation has since launched a new initiative to provide another billion meals by 2035.From 100 million meals to a billionThe original challenge was announced on November 21, 2014. According to a Feeding America announcement, Robbins pledged the equivalent of 50 million meals and invited the public to help match his contribution, bringing the campaign’s target to 100 million meals. The contribution included profits from his recently published book, 'Money: Master the Game', along with an additional personal donation. The food was to be distributed through Feeding America’s network of local food banks. The organisation said the campaign built on Robbins’ longstanding support for hunger relief.The initial target was achieved within two years, according to Feeding America’s later account of the partnership. The campaign then grew beyond its original ambition as Robbins and the organisation sought to reach more families experiencing food insecurity.In 2017, the partnership announced an expanded goal of providing one billion meals by the end of 2025. The campaign relied not only on Robbins’ own contributions but also on donations from individuals who responded to his appeals. His approach included matching gifts and directing proceeds from his books towards hunger relief.The expansion reflected the scale of the problem the initiative was trying to address. Feeding America works through a nationwide network of food banks, food pantries and meal programmes to connect people with food. Its model allows contributions to support distribution through local organisations rather than relying on a single central facility.The billion-meal milestone arrived earlyBy September 2022, the partnership had reported that it had helped provide 914 million meals, putting it well on its way to the billion-meal target. At the time, Robbins and Feeding America said the campaign was ahead of schedule despite rising food and transportation costs placing additional pressure on families and hunger-relief organisations.The goal was formally reached in November 2023, nearly two years before the original 2025 deadline. In its announcement dated November 29, 2023, Feeding America credited Robbins and the thousands of donors who joined the effort. The organisation said the initiative had helped provide one billion meals to people facing hunger across the United States.The campaign’s growth also demonstrated how the original pledge had evolved. Robbins had initially sought to help provide 100 million meals, but the partnership subsequently mobilised additional donations and matching contributions to reach a target ten times larger. Feeding America said Robbins increased his personal and business giving over the years, including a further $10 million contribution during the pandemic.The number represents meals the campaign helped provide, rather than a claim that Robbins personally prepared or distributed a billion individual servings. The initiative depended on donations and the infrastructure of Feeding America’s partner network to turn financial contributions into food assistance.A new billion-meal goal by 2035Reaching the target did not end the partnership. In April 2025, Robbins and Feeding America announced the Next Billion Meals Challenge, a fresh 10-year initiative intended to help provide another billion meals to individuals and families experiencing food insecurity by 2035. According to the announcement, the new effort builds on the earlier campaign and includes a lead matching gift from Robbins to encourage further contributions. The campaign had already helped provide more than 50 million meals when the initiative was announced.Feeding America’s campaign page says every $1 donated helps provide at least 10 meals through its network of food banks. The organisation also describes the new initiative as part of a broader effort to address hunger in the US, while Robbins supports other food-recovery organisations, including FarmLink and Sharing Excess.The US-focused campaign is distinct from the wider 100 Billion Meals Challenge, a global initiative Robbins co-founded with David Beasley, the former executive director of the United Nations World Food Programme. The two efforts have different scopes and should not be confused when assessing the reach of the Feeding America partnership.The memory behind the missionRobbins has repeatedly linked his philanthropy to the Thanksgiving visit that he remembers from childhood. In his account, receiving groceries from a stranger showed him how an act of generosity could change a family’s immediate circumstances and leave a lasting impression. That experience has become a central part of how he explains his commitment to hunger relief. Feeding America’s 2015 annual report records his description of growing up in a food-insecure household and says he had partnered with the organisation to provide meals since 2012. The report also highlights his support for the 100 Million Meals Challenge.The campaign’s trajectory, from a 100-million-meal target announced in 2014 to a billion-meal milestone in 2023—shows how the initial pledge developed into a long-running fundraising partnership. Its next phase sets another billion-meal target for 2035, extending an effort Robbins says was shaped by the help his own family received when he was young.You use AI every day. articles.title: Katie Price denies 'any venom' against ex-husband at his rape trial
articles.summary: Kieran Hayler, who denies offences against a girl when she was 13, was married to Price at the time.
articles.body:
Katie Price has denied having "any venom" against her ex-husband at his rape trial.

Kieran Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one of sexual assault against a then-13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

When challenged by defence lawyer Arlette Piercy on her view of her ex-husband, Price said: "I don't have any venom against Kieran, it was amicable when we split."

Reality star Price also denied being "angry and vengeful" towards Hayler.

During her evidence to Lewes Crown Court, Price was asked by Piercy if she "loved revenge or is it just TV?".

"It's TV, it's what I say. It's what drives me in my work," Price said.

Piercy told Price: "You are angry and vengeful towards the defendant Kieran Hayler, you have evidenced a vendetta against him over a number of years."

Price also said she was using "a figure of speech" when she messaged the teenage girl allegedly raped by her then-husband.

Jurors had previously seen messages sent between Price and the girl, then aged 14, in which the media personality said she had heard Hayler and the girl kissed and he had "tried it on" with her, adding: "I'm only asking as this is a serious allegation."

The teenager replied that it was "just a flirt thing" and "nothing happened".

Price then asked: "Did he kiss you? I won't bring up anymore just want truth. I will make you a little star."

Asked in cross-examination about use of the phrase "little star", Price said: "That's a figure of speech."

Piercy then asked: "When you use that figure of speech, what did you mean?"

Price replied: "I don't know, when she was 13 there's no agenda or nothing behind it.

Hayler, 39, has suggested his ex-wife "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended and the allegations form part of this, the court previously heard.

Hayler was married to media personality Price at the time of the allegations, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021.

The trial previously heard that the alleged victim first contacted the NSPCC in 2021 over the allegations, who then referred her to the police, prompting the investigation.

The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.

articles.title: In Alberta, Canada built an instrumented road with about 825,000 scrap tyres and waste bottom ash, reportedly saving 103,123 m³ of landfill space
articles.summary: Discover how engineers in Edmonton, Alberta, constructed a revolutionary road using nearly one million scrap tires and waste bottom ash, significantly reducing landfill waste and optimizing frost-resistant pavement conditions.
articles.body: Winters in Edmonton are long and cold, and a road there has to cope with ground that freezes deep and then thaws unevenly in spring. Frozen soil under pavement can heave, and as it thaws, it loses strength, so engineers in cold regions look for ways to keep frost away from the soil that supports a road. Meanwhile, scrap tyres accumulate in large numbers, and burning coal for electricity leaves a residue called bottom ash that has to be put somewhere. Researchers at the University of Alberta set out to test whether both materials could go into a single road. They built one that reports its own condition through sensors embedded in the pavement.How the 2012 test road in Edmonton was built and instrumentedThe Integrated Road Research Facility (IRRF) at the University of Alberta, founded in 2012, describes its test road as unique in Canada. The road links the Edmonton Waste Management Centre with Anthony Henday Drive (Highway 216). The road was built with scrap tyres and waste bottom ash and carries more than 250 geotechnical, environmental and pavement sensors, whose data an automated system sends over the Internet to the university laboratory. The IRRF project description states that more than 8,000 tonnes of recycled tyres, about 825,000 scrap tyres, were processed into tyre-derived aggregate and used to build the road. The same description lists three main research areas: tyre-derived aggregate and tyre-soil mixtures as embankment materials, flexible pavement performance in cold weather, and insulated pavement sections using polystyrene boards, bottom ash and tyre-derived aggregate.Landfill savings of 103,123 m³ reported for the Edmonton test roadThe IRRF reports that building the road diverted these tyres from Edmonton’s landfill and saved approximately 103,123 m³ of landfill space. The first published field results came from Negar Tavafzadeh Haghi and colleagues in Using Field Data to Evaluate Bottom Ash as Pavement Insulation Layer, which appeared in Transportation Research Record in 2014.According to the paper, instrumentation took place at various depths in Edmonton, Alberta, and frost depth, freezing, and thawing duration were evaluated using temperature data from October 2012 to June 2013. From the field data, the authors estimated thermal resistivities (R-values) of 1.4 m²°C/W for bottom ash and 16.7 m²°C/W for polystyrene, and the insulation layers reduced frost depth by at least 28% and 40%, respectively, compared with the control pavement section.Frost depth cut by 24% with bottom ash and 64% with polystyrene in the 2021 studyYunyan Huang and colleagues revisited the road eight years after construction in Performance Evaluation of Different Insulating Materials using Field Temperature and Moisture Data, published in Transportation Research Record in 2021. The study took measurements on three 20 m insulated segments and one control segment. Field temperature and moisture gauges were used to compare the 100 cm bottom ash layer with the 10 cm polystyrene board. It was found that the maximum frost depth for the control segment was 2.10 m, 1.60 m with bottom ash, and 0.75 m with polystyrene insulation, a decrease of 24% and 64%, respectively.You use AI every day. articles.title: Argentina moves to stop first commercial oil project on disputed Falkland Islands, escalating row with UK
articles.summary: Argentina on Tuesday said it has approached an international maritime tribunal seeking to halt an oil development project off the disputed Falkland
articles.body: Argentina on Tuesday said it has approached an international maritime tribunal seeking to halt an oil development project off the disputed Falkland Islands, escalating its dispute with the United Kingdom, which controls the archipelago. According to the office of President Javier Milei, Agrentina has filed a request for provisional measures with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg, Germany, seeking to stop the development of Sea Lion, a $2.2-billion Israeli-British oil project north of the Falkland Islands, to “preserve Argentina’s sovereign rights.”Responding to Argentina's move, the UK accused Buenos Aires of taking “measures beyond its jurisdiction” and engaging in “economic coercion”.“The Sea Lion field lies on the Falkland Islands’ continental shelf. The project is lawful and regulated by the democratically elected Falkland Islands government. Argentina has no jurisdiction over it,” UK Foreign Minister Uma Kumaran told the House of Commons on Tuesday.“Let me be absolutely clear: This government will not stand by while Argentina uses economic coercion against the people of the Falkland Islands. We will do whatever it takes to support them,” Kumaran added.The Sea Lion projectThe Sea Lion project is an offshore oilfield located about 220 kilometres (140 miles) north of the Falkland Islands and will be its first commercial oil venture. After years of delays and disruptions, its developers, Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration, expect production to begin in 2028.In recent weeks, Milei has intensified Argentina's claim to the Falklands, describing the islands' nascent oil industry as a “threat” to the country's sovereignty and an attempt to “steal” its natural resources.Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against executives and shareholders involved in the Sea Lion project and proposed legislation to strengthen and expand sanctions against companies and suppliers “exploiting” the Falklands' resources without Argentine authorisation. Analysts say Milei is invoking a cause that enjoys broad political support to shore up his popularity as the economy falters ahead of next year's presidential election.Britain, meanwhile, has defended the islanders' right to develop their natural resources and pledged support for companies operating in the territory.The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea is an independent international court established under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea to resolve disputes over maritime rights. Its rulings are legally binding, but the tribunal has no means of enforcing them if a country refuses to comply.The Falklands disputeThe Falkland Islands remain a longstanding national cause in Argentina, where they are known as the Malvinas. Buenos Aires maintains that the UK has “illegally” occupied the islands since 1833, a claim rejected by London, which cites the islanders' wish to remain a British Overseas Territory.In 1982, Argentina's military dictatorship invaded the archipelago in an attempt to seize it from the UK, triggering a 10-week war that ended in Argentina's surrender. The conflict left 649 Argentine troops, 255 British personnel and three islanders dead.After defeating England in the FIFA World Cup semi-final in July, Argentine players displayed a banner reading “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” (“The Falkland Islands are Argentine”), reiterating the country's longstanding claim to the disputed archipelago.(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. articles.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle, the embattled U.S. ambassador to Greece, said Tuesday that serving in the role “has been the honor of a lifetime” after the White House announced she had been asked to resign. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia shared at her inaugural press briefing that the Trump administration asked Guilfoyle to resign after several…
articles.body:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the embattled U.S. ambassador to Greece, said Tuesday that serving in the role “has been the honor of a lifetime” after the White House announced she had been asked to resign.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia shared at her inaugural press briefing that the Trump administration asked Guilfoyle to resign after several reports alleging misconduct, including asking a GOP donor to pay off a credit card bill.

“I will forever be grateful to President Donald J. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for entrusting me with the extraordinary privilege of representing the greatest country in the history of the world,” Guilfoyle said in a statement posted on social media after Zacharia’s press conference.

“While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end,” she added.

Guilfoyle said that recent allegations against her “are false and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

“I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”

The Wall Street Journal had put out a series of reports about Guilfoyle, including one that she asked Trump donor and supporter Eric Deter to wire her $100,000 to pay off her American Express bill.

In another, the Journal alleged Guilfoyle bragged about her connections to two Greek tycoons who were bankrolling her luxury travel.

Reports had indicated that Trump and Rubio were annoyed over the allegations and were weighing how much longer she would last in the position.

Trump said Monday that they’re “not happy” about the allegations and they were being looked at.

On Tuesday, Trump said he hadn’t spoken with Guilfoyle, but he “didn’t like what I read.”

“She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” he said.

articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday said the stream of negative press stories surrounding the conduct of Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle led to her ousting .

“She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump told reporters outside of the White House.

Trump also played down Guilfoyle’s closeness and history with his family. Guilfoyle was engaged to the president’s son Donald Trump Jr. until 2024, the two were first linked together in 2018. Guilfoyle is also a former Fox News host, one of the president’s favorite news channels.

“She wasn’t a member of my family. I guess she dated my son a long time ago,” Trump said.

The White House announced Tuesday the president had asked for Guilfoyle’s resignation , and she posted a statement to the social media platform X shortly after the news broke.

Trump said he hadn’t spoken to Guilfoyle.

“I didn’t speak to her. But she won’t be there. I didn’t like what I read,” Trump said.

Guilfoyle’s ousting came after a series of reports detailing embarrassing, or possibly illegal, activity ahead of her confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece and during her more than year-long tenure.

This included a Wall Street Journal report detailing Guilfoyle’s close relationship with a lobbyist representing a Greek shipping firm , in which she had the lobbyist participate in high-level meetings, consistently promoted his firm and accepted private flights paid for by the company.

A second Journal report revealed text messages between Guilfoyle and a Trump donor, with the ambassadorial nominee raising concern that their communications could tank her confirmation. She solicited the donor, Eric Deters , for $100,000 to pay down her credit card debt. Deters said that Guilfoyle promised to advocate for Deters with top Trump officials in exchange for money, the Journal reported.

A third Journal report published Sunday detailed Guilfoyle boasting about close ties to Greek shipping tycoons who were bankrolling her lavish travel.

Guilfoyle, in a statement on X, rejected any allegations of wrongdoing and said that while her time as ambassador to Greece was ending, she would continue being an advocate for Trump and his political movement.

“While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end,” she wrote.

articles.title: Iran targeting military sites in UK, MI5 chief says
articles.summary: Iran has ramped up attempts to hit military installations in the United Kingdom, with the suspected plot to attack a U.S.-run air base last month part of a broader effort of attacks by Tehran, according to the head of Britain’s MI5 spy agency. Threats to British military sites, intelligence facilities and high-security targets are a…
articles.body:
Iran has ramped up attempts to hit military installations in the United Kingdom, with the suspected plot to attack a U.S.-run air base last month part of a broader effort of attacks by Tehran, according to the head of Britain’s MI5 spy agency.

Threats to British military sites, intelligence facilities and high-security targets are a “major shift this year” in “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets,” MI5 Director General Ken McCallum said in a Tuesday speech.

McCallum pointed to the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in southern England on Sept. 27, saying it was “not unique.” He said there have “been other examples” of such threats to sites “not just in the U.K. but around the world, most particularly in Iran’s own region.”

The threat against RAF Fairford, reported to be a potential drone attack ordered by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, prompted the U.S. military to hastily relocate the 12 Air Force B-1 bombers stationed there, moving them back to home stations in the U.S. The American bombers have been stationed at the base in support of the Trump administration’s war in Iran, now in its eighth month.

British authorities said they had thwarted an alleged terrorist plot, initially arresting five men on explosives and terror charges near the air base. The men, all five of whom are British nationals in their 20s, were released on bail a day later. Two additional men have since been arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts but also were released on bail.

Iran has denied any connection to the suspected plot.

In his Tuesday speech, meant to outline significant threats to the U.K., McCallum said British authorities have made more than 50 arrests in “Iran-linked operations” in the past 12 months.

But the suspected plot against RAF Fairford marks an escalation from lower-level attacks including arson and stabbings, carried out by Iranian proxies and targeting Jewish communities, according to McCallum.

The U.K. faces a “new era of national security,” he said, with Russia and Iran increasing their hybrid warfare campaigns against the country.

He assured the audience, however, that given what British authorities have seen in practice, Iran has not shown “anywhere near the level of capability” to launch a sophisticated attack on U.K. military installations or other such sites.

articles.title: The AI race with China the US is losing
articles.summary: While the U.S. focuses on frontier AI technology, China is gaining dominance in the Global South by providing affordable, open-weight models and cloud infrastructure, posing long-term risks to American economic interests and national security.
articles.body:
Much of the AI discussion in the U.S. has centered on the need to win the technology race with China. While the U.S. is focused on achieving the most advanced frontier AI technologies, we are losing the global market to China.

Most of the world is not looking for the most cutting-edge frontier model. They are looking for something they can afford and that works. While the U.S. is investing in the most advanced technologies, China is actively pushing its cheaper models around the developing world. Losing this race will have long-term negative implications for the United States.

The competition in these countries will help determine whether U.S. or Chinese technology runs their infrastructure, supports their hospitals and classrooms, and delivers government services.

As Chinese products and services are brought in to run infrastructure, classrooms, airports, and government services across Africa, Asia and Latin America, China is building long-term relationships that will be difficult for the U.S. to penetrate.

Purchasing Chinese technology also brings risks. Chinese technology may be less secure than American technology, creating potential national security threats. China also frequently sells technology that enables countries to surveil their populations.

By focusing on open-weight models , China is making its technology easier for others to adopt. Unlike many American models, which are only available through services controlled by their companies, Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Alibaba’s models are available for others to download and adapt .

Huawei is already expanding its significant footprint throughout the Global South. In April, Huawei announced AI services in nine additional countries , including Brazil, Indonesia, and South Africa, offering access to DeepSeek and other Chinese models through its cloud network. In Egypt, Huawei offered eligible startups up to $150,000 in cloud credits to help pay for computing services, along with training and an Arabic-language model. These offers lower the cost of getting started and encourage local companies to build around Chinese technology.

Microsoft estimated that DeepSeek usage in Africa was two to four times higher than in other regions during the second half of 2025. Its report also pointed to the free access and partnerships that DeepSeek offers to distribute its technology.

Chinese cloud providers are also expanding globally, with a particular focus on emerging markets . In Latin America, a 2025 study found that Chinese data center providers accounted for 25 percent of the market in Brazil, 40 percent in Chile, and 100 percent in Argentina, Mexico and Peru. The same study found that Chinese companies owned 57 percent of the data center market in Indonesia and 100 percent in Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia.

As Chinese suppliers become the main providers of AI across developing economies, Beijing will be able to wield more influence in those countries. Once a government builds public services around a supplier’s systems, changing providers can become costly and disruptive. If essential services rely on Chinese suppliers for computing and technical support, a country may find it harder to challenge Beijing on other issues. Commercial choices made today could influence political choices tomorrow.

There are risks to information as well. U.S. government testing found that the DeepSeek models it examined repeated misleading Chinese Communist Party narratives more often than American comparison models. As people increasingly turn to AI to understand history and current events, those answers could give Beijing’s preferred version of the world a wider audience.

Finally, American businesses will lose future sales of software, computing equipment, and services, hampering their long-term viability and narrowing opportunities for the workers who build and support those products.

The expansion of China’s scientific and technological cooperation with the Global South has long been a priority for the Chinese government through its Digital Silk Road strategy, together with extensive financing to support and subsidize Chinese companies .

The loss of the U.S. Agency for International Development and the lack of a coordinated U.S. government approach to the Global South are hampering the development of a coherent strategy. The U.S. should make affordable access to AI and technology a central goal of its work with developing countries.

The U.S. has begun responding by promoting packages of American AI technology and making export financing more readily available. But these steps are not enough to compete with China in countries with limited budgets.

The U.S. should significantly increase the funding available to countries interested in purchasing U.S. AI and technology. It should also invest in training the people who will be the local users, partner with countries to train developers, support tools in local languages, and work with partner governments to identify problems they need to solve.

China is ahead in the technology race in the Global South, and the U.S. must move quickly to ensure that it does not lose the global AI race. Losing that race would have serious consequences for U.S. influence, national security, and our ability to shape how AI is developed and used around the world.

Orit Frenkel is CEO of the American Leadership Initiative.

articles.title: In 2025, South Korea approved a two-year test near Osong Station for solar panels placed along railway tracks, with nationwide expansion possible if the panels withstand rail conditions
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking move, South Korea has approved a two-year pilot project utilizing removable solar panels along railway tracks near Osong Station, potentially revolutionizing renewable energy generation in the rail sector. This initiative could pave the way for nationwide expansion if successful.
articles.body: Railways were built to move people and goods, but engineers are now asking whether the tracks themselves can do more. The space between the rails is long, flat, already cleared and part of the railway property. A Swiss startup called Sun-Ways has spent several years working out how to fill that space with removable solar panels without getting in the way of trains.In September 2025, South Korea's Korea Railway Solar Power Generation Project received government approval to install solar panels near Osong Station in North Chungcheong Province. According to Swissinfo's reporting, the pilot will run for two years, with nationwide expansion possible if it performs well.Where is the pilot project located?Details on the Korean site are scant. Swissinfo said it was near Osong Station, and the Irish Times said the two-year pilot was approved for the Korea Railroad Research Institute’s test track, which makes sense as the institute has a railroad test track at Osong. The project is being conducted by the Korean Rail Solar Power Generation Project Company, whose chief executive, Taebon Park, told Swissinfo in 2025 that he opted for Sun-Ways because the technology is suitable for railroad maintenance and operations. Park attended the Swiss inauguration and was particularly interested in how the panels connect electrically and how they move on and off the track.It helps to be clear on what the panels are and aren’t. They are not on the poles along the line. In the Sun-Ways design, they sit on the sleepers between the rails and are held in place by pistons pushing on the steel, as the Irish Times put it. Sun-Ways estimates that Switzerland's roughly 5,320 kilometres of railway network, excluding tunnels and poorly lit sections, could generate up to 1 billion kilowatt-hours of solar electricity annually. That is equivalent to approximately 188 megawatt-hours per kilometre per year and represents the company's estimate for suitable routes.Lessons in SwitzerlandKorea is participating in a study that has been underway in Switzerland for more than a year. Sun-Ways launched the pilot on April 24, 2025, installing 48 removable solar panels across a 100-meter stretch of an active passenger railway line in Buttes, in the canton of Neuchâtel, Switzerland. The installation consists of 48 panels, each rated at 380 watts, giving a total peak output of around 18 kilowatts. France's SNCF Group is working with Sun-Ways to assess how the removable solar panels affect railway maintenance and operations. Its teams are examining panel installation and removal, glare, track inspections, maintenance impacts, electricity output and dirt buildup. According to SNCF's official project page, the pilot will run until April 2028. A trial in Korea will demonstrate how the system can cope with local climate and operating conditions. No performance data from the Korean site have been made public at the time of writing; thus, the results from Osong remain to be seen.Can South Korea’s rail network afford it?A separate modelling study examined the potential for generating solar power on suitable railway corridors in South Korea. The researchers estimated the system's potential electricity output and assessed its financial viability, but they did not measure the performance of the Osong pilot itself.The South Korean modelling study identified 28.4 kilometres of suitable railway corridor, with an estimated solar capacity of 8.51 megawatts and annual electricity generation of 9.95 gigawatt-hours. That works out to approximately 350 megawatt-hours per kilometre annually. The estimate is higher than Sun-Ways' projection of roughly 188 megawatt-hours per kilometre, but the two figures rely on different system configurations and installed-capacity assumptions. They should not be treated as directly equivalent measurements. The study's figures describe a modelled system, not electricity production measured at the Osong pilot.The modelling study estimated a 68% probability of payback within 12 years when the proposed system received a 40% capital subsidy, compared with roughly one-third without the subsidy. These figures represent a modelled financial scenario, not a requirement that removable panels remain on the same stretch of railway for 12 years. The overall investment case depends on factors such as installation and removal costs, maintenance, electricity generation and the assumptions used in the model.Meanwhile, Sun-Ways says it is transitioning from pilot to commercial rollout. The Greater Geneva Bern area, a Swiss business development agency, said in August 2026 that the firm has signed its first commercial partner in Italy, has a technological partnership with SNCF and has obtained South Korean permission. China, Singapore and Indonesia are also interested.South Korea approves a pilot for solar panels between railway rails near Osong Station, using Swiss technology already running on a live line in Switzerland. Nobody yet knows how the Korean panels will perform, but the Swiss results, the modelling study showing real potential and a tough payback, and the shortage of land for solar farms help explain why the idea is spreading. If the Osong pilot performs well, it could support a wider rollout across the country’s rail network.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump: China, Russia ‘have too much to lose’ to help Iran
articles.summary: President Trump late Monday accused China and Russia of having “too much to lose” to enable Iran in the ongoing conflict. “I see so many comments from the Radical Left Morons and Lunatics that China and Russia are helping the ‘wonderful’ Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “If they are, it’s at…
articles.body:
President Trump late Monday accused China and Russia of having “too much to lose” to enable Iran in the ongoing conflict .

“I see so many comments from the Radical Left Morons and Lunatics that China and Russia are helping the ‘wonderful’ Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “If they are, it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all.”

He added, “They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!”

The president made a similar argument in July, saying at the time that he took the testimony from the leaders of China and Russia that they are not providing Iran with weapons at face value, adding that it “would be very bad for them” if they had.

This came after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers on Capitol Hill that China and Russia were “enabling them.”

Reports over the course of the war have suggested that both countries have aided Tehran.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC News’s Kristen Welker in March that “military cooperation between Iran and Russia is not something new. It’s not a secret.” He did not describe what that cooperation looks like when pressed by Welker, amid rumors that Russia was providing Iran with intelligence.

CNN reported in April that China prepared to deliver new air defense systems to Iran, according to sources familiar with U.S. intelligence assessments. One source told the outlet that Beijing could route the defense shipments through third countries to obscure their source of origin. These defense systems were expected to reach Iran in September, according to Reuters .

The U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran has stretched into its eighth month. The war, broadly unpopular among Americans, led prices at the gas pump to soar — primarily after Iran implemented an effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil is transported.

The prolonged war has spurred mounting concerns about diminished U.S. weapons stockpiles and the steep cost to friendly countries in the region.

Trump’s latest response to the energy crisis was a deal with Russia to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplaces. The Friday announcement spurred backlash from lawmakers, with a group of six Republican senators calling the deal “ a betrayal of our allies ” while the U.S. backs Ukraine in its war against Moscow.

The president and other administration officials have argued that U.S. strikes have severely diminished Iran’s military capacity as part of the objective of stopping Iran’s nuclear program. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent echoed the comments Sunday when asked about the ongoing military operation, one that Trump and other officials predicted would be short and last weeks .

“I don’t know what ‘crying uncle’ is in Farsi, but they’re going to be crying uncle,” Bessent told Fox News’s Rachel Campos-Duffy on “Fox & Friends Weekend.”

“You know, they are collapsing. They can’t pay their soldiers. And Rachel, I don’t know how this ends,” he added. “You never know how this ends.”

articles.title: Argentina targets UK in legal claim over Falklands oil exploration
articles.summary: The action filed with an international maritime tribunal is the latest development in an escalating row over the Falkland Islands.
articles.body:
The Argentinian government has begun legal action seeking to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields north of the Falkland Islands in an escalating row with the UK.

Buenos Aires said in a statement the request lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea aimed to block activity authorised "illegally" by the UK.

The claim comes a fortnight after Argentinian President Javier Milei demanded the scrapping of the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies.

UK Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran criticised the "escalating campaign" from Argentina against companies operating in the Falklands, while announcing new protections for them.

The developments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the self-governing British territory, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentinian forces which had invaded the territory.

Earlier last month Milei also threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands.

Uma Kumaran accused the Argentinian government of "economic coercion" against the people of the Falkland Islands.

"We will do whatever it takes to support them," she told the House of Commons on Tuesday.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

The Falkland Islands government extended exploration licences last month and the field is expected to start pumping in 2028, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – have insisted they have valid licences issued by Britain.

The Argentinian government claims the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.

Its application "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorised unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom".

In a post on X, Argentinian Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno said the government was requesting the tribunal make a number of orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits.

But the UK government insists Sea Lion is lawful, located on the Falkland Islands shelf and regulated by the islands' government.

While the Falkland Islands government grants exploration licences, they must be signed off by the UK Foreign Secretary.

Kumaran said the tribunal application "does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease".

The tribunal that will consider the dispute is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

FCDO officials have made clear the UK will engage with the tribunal but resist Argentina's claim firmly.

They said the aim was not to escalate the dispute but respond firmly to Argentina's latest move, and defend what the UK sees as legitimate economic activity.

They also hope to provide reassurance to businesses fearful of Argentine retribution. That is why they are introducing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests Act that would protect firms from any extra-territorial impact of Argentine laws following Milei's sanctions threats.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Argentina's attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion."

The latest move comes after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly late last month for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.

He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".

On Tuesday Kumaran described Milei's remarks at New York as "inflammatory".

Despite its defeat in 1982, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falkland Islands. But over the years successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.

UK officials believes the current Argentine leadership is deliberately picking a fight ahead of elections next year.

articles.title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis sentenced to 40 years for rapper Tupac Shakur's murder
articles.summary: Davis was found guilty last month over his role in the late rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in 1996.
articles.body:
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.

A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime.

Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world".

Ex-gang boss guilty of orchestrating 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur

Tupac murder trial: 'All hell broke loose' night of rapper's shooting, witness says

Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, told the court: "The loss of Tupac, for a long time, crippled my family."

"He had so much promise, intentions for a better world," said adding that her brother had hoped to help his local community.

Sekyiwa Shakur asked the judge to give Davis the maximum sentence, telling Davis he will sit in prison and "contemplate what you've done to the world, not just to me".

Shakur's brother, Maurice Shakur, also addressed the court, asking the judge for "the longest possible sentence".

Davis was asked by Judge Carli Kierny if he had anything to say, to which he replied: "I'm good. I'm gonna appeal this case for sure."

Before handing down the sentence, Kierny told him: "You don't get to take a man from his family.

"You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur. The world never forgot about him and his death."

The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.

In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview relating to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur.

Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews.

But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him.

Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.

For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month.

Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.

Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

articles.title: EU watchdog urges smart glasses to clearly signal when recording
articles.summary: Advisory comes amid growing concern about the devices being used to secretly record girls and women.
articles.body:
The European Union’s data watchdog has called for smart glasses to clearly show when they are recording, saying bystanders have the right to know when they are being photographed or filmed.

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued the non-binding recommendation on Tuesday, amid mounting concern about the devices being used to secretly record girls and women.

It said the use of smart glasses – which can resemble ordinary glasses but also take photos and videos, make phone calls and translate text when connected to the internet – raises “serious privacy concerns”.

EDPB chair Anu Talus said the glasses should have clear signals when they are recording, such as “bright LED lights, audio signals or voice activation cues, privacy-friendly smartphone notifications, or unique designs”.

“These warnings need to be reliable, hard to ignore, and always up to date,” said Talus. “Even in public spaces, bystanders should clearly understand that someone is filming or photographing them.”

The devices carry greater risks in “sensitive” spaces like schools and hospitals, as well as public spots like beaches, and raised concerns about children who are “more vulnerable to covert or intrusive processing of their personal data”, the EDPB warned.

The advisory comes amid campaigns in several European countries to ban or restrict smart glasses over privacy concerns.

Norway’s government said last week it was also worried about privacy invasions and wants a temporary ban on the use of smart glasses in certain public places. The capital Oslo already opted to ban glasses equipped with cameras in schools.

France’s e-Enfance association, which operates the national hotline for victims of online abuse, has also sounded the alarm about videos recorded with camera-equipped glasses and shared online.

Last month, French prosecutors said they had opened a criminal probe ⁠following sexual harassment complaints related to a social media trend of using smart glasses to film women on the street, without their consent, and posting the videos online.

In the United Kingdom and Ireland, a “Stop Smart Glasses” campaign has launched a petition and call for supporters to contact stores to stop their sale. It reached more than 10,000 signatures, which means the UK government must respond.

articles.title: Trump says Houthis trying to increase oil prices before US elections
articles.summary: US president suggests that Yemen-based group are ‘purposefully trying to drive up oil prices’ before November vote.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has said that the Houthi rebel group in Yemen are stepping up attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia in a bid to increase energy prices in the run-up to the US midterm elections.

Trump said on Tuesday that the Houthis were behaving “very badly” and repeated his threat that the US could step up military attacks across the Middle East after the November elections .

“They’ve [the Houthis] been silent for a long time, but now they’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran, which is a Failing Nation, with No Navy, No Airforce, the World’s Worst Economy, and 301 percent Inflation, in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the US Elections,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “NOT NICE.”

Trump’s decision to launch a war on Iran with Israel in February has caused surging energy prices and rising concerns about cost of living issues in the US, where voters will soon decide whether the president’s Republican Party maintains its majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Democrats hope to capitalise on the president’s unpopularity and voter frustration over the war and rising costs to seize control of one or both houses of Congress, allowing them to block Trump’s legislative agenda for the remainder of his time in office.

Trump added on Tuesday that he would “never forget” the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, seeming to threaten renewed US military attacks after the midterms, widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term.

“Somebody should explain to them [the Houthis] that I’m not running in the Elections, I’ve already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE, but I’ll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!” he said.

Polls have shown that Trump’s war on Iran is deeply unpopular , with a recent AP-NORC poll finding that nearly 70 percent of voters say the war was not worth fighting.

Trump has dismissed unfavourable polls as “fake” and pointed to crowds at his political rallies as proof of his popularity.

articles.title: Musician Kacey Musgraves condemns Columbus as 'the lamest person to probably ever exist'
articles.summary: Kacey Musgraves blasted Christopher Columbus onstage in Texas and also recently hosted Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at a concert.
articles.body: Singer-songwriter Kacey Musgraves blasted Italian explorer Christopher Columbus shortly before Columbus Day. As she spoke to the Texas crowd during her second night at American Airlines Center Sunday, Musgraves noted that the next day, Monday, was Columbus Day. "Tomorrow’s Monday? … Ew, that’s right, wait, it’s Columbus Day? It’s what now?" she asked as the audience booed and corrected her, saying it is Indigenous People’s Day. "Yeah, no yeah yeah, actually, obviously f--- Columbus. Literally the lamest person to probably ever exist. Like for real. What a loser," she said. "You’re a loser, Christopher Columbus, we hate you!" GOO GOO DOLLS' JOHN RZEZNIK DRAWS LINE ON POLITICS AT CONCERTS: 'I'M NOT GOING TO LECTURE YOU' While revered for his voyages across the Atlantic Ocean that paved the way for European exploration in the Americas, Columbus has also been heavily scrutinized by activists and academics over his treatment of Indigenous people and the start of mass colonization. As a result, in recent decades there have been repeated flare-ups of national tension over whether the explorer should be celebrated. Musgraves has made headlines recently for her political activism. In August, she had urged her fans to donate to Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights. "It’s a wonderful organization, and they help give aid — legal aid — and money to children whose parents have been deported unfairly," Musgraves said. "It’s not a political thing. It’s just, these kids need help." More recently, Newsweek reported that Musgraves hosted Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at a concert in Dallas over the weekend, siding with him as she mocked former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. SKILLET FRONTMAN JOHN COOPER TALKS ABOUT THE RISKS OF TALKING POLITICS AND WHY HE WANTS TO 'STAY IN HIS LANE' Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under President Donald Trump, spoke to Fox News Digital, defending Columbus and arguing Musgraves is off the mark. "Obviously, no one expects a corporate-backed recording star to know a damn thing about world history, but, unfortunately, the abysmal educational standards of our public schools have made Musgrave’s misinformed views widespread among regular Americans. "That’s the real problem. Columbus was a courageous adventurer and ahead-of-his-time navigator to whom we owe much of the prosperity we now enjoy. The kind of prosperity that makes it possible for Musgraves to rake in millions while spouting uneducated hot takes with no basis in reality." articles.title: OpenAI employee arrested over hidden listening device, company says
articles.summary: OpenAI said on Tuesday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation had arrested one of its employees in connection with a sophisticated listening device found hidden in one of the company’s offices.
articles.body: OpenAI said on Tuesday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation had arrested one of its employees in connection with a sophisticated listening device found hidden in one of the company’s offices. The ChatGPT maker had used its internal AI models to identify the individual responsible for planting the device and to trace its origins, it said in an X post. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” according to the AI company. OpenAI personnel discovered the audio recording device inserted into a USB port of a television in an executive conference room inside an OpenAI building in San Francisco, according to a news release from the Justice Department. The device had been concealed in toilet paper and installed “on or about Sept. 28.” It was discovered “on or about Sept. 30,” the Justice Department said. Meetings that occur in the conference room where the device was discovered frequently involved discussions of “highly confidential” and “nonpublic” information, the Justice Department added. OpenAI said its security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats. The company said it referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The 35-year-old man from Saudi Arabia, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on Oct. 9 and made his initial appearance in federal court today, the Justice Department said. His employment was also terminated on Oct. 9 after the company took “gradual steps to contain the risk while the investigation continued,” including restricting the employee’s access and placing him on leave, according to OpenAI. Alfozan was hired as an engineer by OpenAI in July 2025, according to the criminal complaint. FBI Director Kash Patel said Alfozan “allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology.” OpenAI said it has evidence that the employee “intended to deploy other recording devices.” The complaint alleges that Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building on Oct. 5, which “OpenAI security personnel found and opened,” discovering a similar recording device. OpenAI faces scrutiny over security incidents involving its AI systems. Reuters and other media outlets reported recently that the company had told investors its annualized revenue for September was almost $50 billion, a drop from what it signaled earlier. OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers after an investigation found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information. The statement came after the researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture that had allowed researchers to raise safety concerns. Alfozan is scheduled to appear in federal court again on Oct. 19.
